readme: What the research literature leads us to expect when a person's depressive symptoms are worse, for each thing the app measures. 'expected' is the direction of the measure when symptoms are WORSE: lower, higher, or mixed (reports disagree). 'support' is our own rough grade of how well established the expectation is: stronger, moderate, weaker, mixed. These are hypotheses to test within one person over time. They are not diagnostic rules. Reviewed by a clinician: no. The reference notes name the line of research; the exact papers must be checked before this is cited anywhere.

note_mood_low.label: Share of notes and check-ins labelled low

features.label: Time spent smiling
features.why: Fewer and shorter smiles are among the most repeated findings in observational studies of depression.
features.reference_note: Facial action coding studies of clinical interviews (Cohn, Girard and colleagues).

features.label: Smiles per minute
features.why: Same finding as time spent smiling, counted as events.
features.reference_note: As above.

features.label: Smile intensity
features.why: Smiles that do occur tend to be weaker.
features.reference_note: As above.

features.label: Smiles that reach the eyes
features.why: Smiles with cheek raise (Duchenne smiles) are reported as reduced; mouth-only smiles may be kept for social reasons.
features.reference_note: Work on Duchenne and non-Duchenne smiles in depression.

features.label: Smiled at a pleasant moment
features.why: Reduced reactivity to positive events is a core feature of anhedonia; the measure is a smile shortly after a marked pleasant moment in the activity.
features.reference_note: Emotion context insensitivity and positive attenuation literature.

features.label: Delay before smiling at a pleasant moment
features.why: Slowed or blunted positive response.
features.reference_note: Inferred from reactivity and psychomotor findings; little direct evidence.

features.label: Overall facial movement
features.why: Reduced facial expressiveness (flat affect, psychomotor retardation) is a long-standing clinical observation and is found in automated analyses.
features.reference_note: Psychomotor retardation literature; automated facial analysis in depression.

features.label: Brows drawn down
features.why: More brow lowering has been reported in some studies of sadness and distress; findings are not consistent.
features.reference_note: Facial action unit 4 in depression; mixed results.

features.label: Inner brows raised
features.why: The inner brow raise is part of the sadness expression.
features.reference_note: Facial action unit 1; limited evidence in everyday settings.

features.label: Blink rate
features.why: Both higher and lower blink rates have been reported; blink rate also depends strongly on the task, screen distance and fatigue.
features.reference_note: Blink rate studies in mood disorders; inconsistent.

features.label: Blink length
features.why: Longer blinks go with fatigue and lowered arousal.
features.reference_note: Mostly fatigue research; indirect.

features.label: Time looking down
features.why: Gaze aversion and downward gaze are part of the non-verbal picture of depression. In a phone task the screen position confounds this.
features.reference_note: Gaze and head pose studies in depression (Alghowinem and colleagues, among others).

features.label: Head angle (down is higher)
features.why: A lowered head posture is reported in depression.
features.reference_note: Head pose studies in depression.

features.label: Head movement
features.why: Reduced head motion is reported with greater severity.
features.reference_note: Automated head motion analysis in clinical interviews (Girard and colleagues).

features.label: Reaction time to embers (at most 6 taps a game)
features.why: Slowing in thinking and movement is well documented with tasks of many trials. This game gives two to six taps, so it is a rough reading of that.
features.reference_note: Processing speed and psychomotor slowing in major depression; redefined for Revontulet on 14 November 2026.

features.label: Variability of reaction time (this game gives too few taps)
features.why: More variable responding goes with lapses of attention, but a spread needs many taps and a game has six at most.
features.reference_note: Intra-individual variability in depression; redefined for Revontulet on 14 November 2026.

features.label: Embers missed
features.why: Attention is often reduced, with small effects in short tasks. Here it is embers not tapped out of those shown; no wrong tap is possible.
features.reference_note: Attention in depression; redefined for Revontulet on 14 November 2026.

features.label: Activities finished
features.why: Lower motivation and energy; also depends on the day and the task.
features.reference_note: Engagement in digital interventions; indirect.

features.label: Good things named in the check-in
features.why: Less positive recall and anhedonia.
features.reference_note: Positive memory bias literature; indirect.

features.label: Plans carried out
features.why: Behavioural activation research: fewer planned pleasant activities are carried out when symptoms are worse.
features.reference_note: Behavioural activation.

features.label: Steps per day
features.why: Lower physical activity is consistently associated with more depressive symptoms.
features.reference_note: Actigraphy and passive sensing studies.

features.label: Walking speed
features.why: Slower gait is reported in depression.
features.reference_note: Gait studies in depression.

features.label: Sleep hours
features.why: Both short and long sleep occur; variability matters more than the mean.
features.reference_note: Sleep in depression.

features.label: Heart-rate variability
features.why: Lower heart-rate variability is associated with depression in meta-analyses, with small effects.
features.reference_note: Heart-rate variability meta-analyses.

caveats.few_sessions: Too few sessions for a stable estimate.
caveats.no_reference_rating: No clinical rating available; only proxies were used.
caveats.proxy_shares_cause: The proxy and the measure may both move for the same everyday reason.
caveats.poor_tracking: Many sessions had poor face tracking.
caveats.task_confound: The measure depends on how the phone is held or where the screen is.
caveats.time_of_day: Sessions were at different times of day.
caveats.novelty: Early sessions differ because the activity was new.
caveats.fatigue_or_illness: Tiredness or physical illness can produce the same picture.
caveats.medication: Medication can change facial movement, blinking and reaction time.
caveats.glasses_or_light: Glasses or lighting can change what the camera measures.
caveats.many_tests: Many measures were tested; some will look related by chance.
caveats.mixed_literature: The research literature itself disagrees on this measure.
caveats.single_person: This is one person's pattern over time, not evidence about people in general.
